record.paper_title: Open problems in microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion
record.original_question: What microscopic mechanism produces the oblate-prolate asymmetry in nuclear structure, meaning the empirical tendency for prolate shapes to be energetically favored over oblate shapes in many nuclei, especially in gamma-soft situations where large-amplitude shape mixing can easily wash out separate rotational-band identities?

evidence.quote: In spite of the obvious importance for understanding low-energy collective spectra, the microscopic origin of the oblate-prolate asymmetry in nuclear structure (the reason why the prolate shapes are energetically more favored in many cases than the oblate shapes) still remains as one of the long-standing and fundamental problems.
It may be interesting to apply this approach to the problem in question for a deeper understanding of the oblate-prolate asymmetry.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In the nuclear shell model and the theory of nuclear collective motion, a deformed nucleus can be characterized (to leading order) by a quadrupole deformation parameter whose sign distinguishes prolate (cigar-shaped, axially elongated) from oblate (disk-shaped, axially flattened) intrinsic shapes. Empirically, across the chart of nuclides, ground-state deformations of even–even nuclei show a pronounced bias toward prolate shapes, even though a naive symmetric treatment of the quadrupole degree of freedom would treat the two signs of deformation on an equal footing. This prolate dominance persists, and indeed becomes especially subtle to identify, in gamma-soft regimes where large-amplitude fluctuations in the triaxiality degree of freedom mix prolate and oblate configurations and blur distinct rotational bands.

Problem. Starting from a microscopic, fully self-consistent many-nucleon framework (for instance, a nuclear energy-density functional or a realistic effective Hamiltonian together with a treatment of large-amplitude collective motion that goes beyond the static mean field, such as the adiabatic self-consistent collective coordinate method or generator-coordinate-type approaches incorporating triaxial and pairing degrees of freedom), identify and quantitatively explain the microscopic mechanism responsible for the systematic energetic preference of prolate over oblate intrinsic quadrupole deformations in the ground states of even–even nuclei. The explanation should:

(i) Derive the asymmetry between the two signs of axial quadrupole deformation from properties of the nucleon-nucleon effective interaction and single-particle structure (e.g., spin–orbit coupling, the orbital ℓ² term, surface diffuseness, pairing), rather than postulating it through asymmetric phenomenological terms.

(ii) Account for the observed dependence of prolate-versus-oblate preference on mass number, neutron and proton numbers relative to magic numbers, and shell filling.

(iii) Remain valid in gamma-soft and shape-coexisting situations, where large-amplitude shape mixing can erase the identity of separate rotational bands, by predicting the asymmetry as a property of the full collective potential and inertia on the (β,γ) shape manifold rather than of a single static minimum.
artifact.status_search_result: Several partial microscopic explanations exist (e.g., Tajima–Suzuki interference of spin–orbit and ℓ² terms in the Nilsson potential, surface-diffuseness arguments, and SU(3) higher-order interacting-boson-model treatments that break prolate–oblate mirror symmetry). These reproduce prolate dominance under certain conditions, but no single microscopic derivation from a fundamental nucleon–nucleon interaction quantitatively accounts for the global systematics, and recent works (2023–2024) continue to revisit the prolate–oblate asymmetry, indicating that a complete explanation remains open.

status_evidence.title: Prolate dominance of nuclear shape caused by a strong interference between the effects of spin-orbit and l^2 terms of the Nilsson potential
status_evidence.snippet: Prolate-shape dominance is realized at the proper strength of the spin-orbit potential together with the standard surface diffuseness.
status_evidence.claim: A partial microscopic mechanism (spin–orbit and ℓ² interference in the Nilsson potential) has been proposed.

status_evidence.title: Prolate-oblate asymmetric shape phase transition in the interacting boson model with SU(3) higher-order interactions
status_evidence.snippet: An IBM with SU(3) higher-order interactions in which prolate and oblate shapes are not described in a mirror-symmetric way.
status_evidence.claim: Recent (2023) work still actively models prolate–oblate asymmetry, indicating the question is not fully closed.

status_evidence.title: Prolate-oblate shape transitions and O(6) symmetry in even-even nuclei: A theoretical overview
status_evidence.snippet: Theoretical overview of prolate–oblate shape transitions in even-even nuclei.
status_evidence.claim: A 2024 overview indicates the topic remains an active area of investigation.
